adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Sorry, I mistook you, 's all."
adjudicated.assessment: The full exchange immediately completes the apparent ellipsis: GHS says I mistook you, Taichi asks For what?, and Nanaka answers A different one. The surrounding turns establish mistaken identity rather than contradicting it, so the original finding was based on an isolated line.

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "For what?"
adjudicated.assessment: For what? is an elliptical response to I mistook you, and the next line A different one answers that exact question. The wording is terse, but context makes the intended mistook me for what relation functional rather than changing it into a purpose question.

adjudicated.jp: 「対等でないと合わせる顔がないってことでしょ？」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "You're saying you're too ashamed to even look at her face because you're not equal, don't you see?"

adjudicated.jp: 「裏返せば、相手にも自分と対等になって欲しいってことだ」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "If you look it from the opposite side, it's wanting the other side to become equal to yourself, that's what."
comments: Well, no. If Taichi can't even look at Youko, then the implication is always inferiority, even when superiority is stated. No need to get in cultural polemics: since Taichi correctly believes Youko to be a wimp underneath it all, this may just be an implication of that reality. And, also, that Taichi can't look at Youko because he's the one who killed her, provided she ever existed at all. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: 裏返せば means 'conversely' or 'looked at the other way.' The English construction lacks the required preposition after 'look' and literalizes a side.

highlights.text: If you look it from the opposite side

adjudicated.jp: 「ピーナッツ入り柿の種の尊厳を認めるんなら、弱い相手を弱いまま認めないとオカシイんじゃないかな」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "If you can accept that there's dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon, then not accepting a weak companion that stays weak is kinda odd isn't it."
comments: Told you they were important. See above for the weakness part. If one can accept peanuts as seeds of persimmon, then one can accept as human what, by the standards of the world, isn't. This would mean Taichi has not forgiven Youko for what she did, not yet at least. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese invokes the dignity of Kaki no Tane with peanuts: the mixed snack as a whole. GHS instead says the dignity lies in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon, turning the product name into a name for its peanuts and misreading the possessive structure.
adjudicated.remedy: Refer to the dignity of Kaki no Tane with peanuts, or of the peanut-and-rice-cracker mix as a whole.

highlights.text: dignity in referring to peanuts as Seeds of Persimmon

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "Ain't it. Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho."
comments: If Nanaka points to the hokora, and Sakuraba points to Nanaka... -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: In context, Ain't it functions as rough agreement, while Kaki no Tane's Sakuraba thing tho compresses the idea that the Kaki no Tane argument was Sakuraba's. The phrasing is highly marked, but it preserves the attribution rather than mapping Sakuraba onto an ingredient or reversing the exchange.
adjudicated.remedy: No source-bound correction required; a cleaner stylistic rendering would be Right. Though the Kaki no Tane speech was Sakuraba's.

comments: Think about this for a second: what mother would really be happy for her son to be an antisocial recluse? "Not qualified for human relationships" doesn't mean that; it means he's someone who seeks something higher than what's available in the world. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese says she is happy if Taichi shares her view. The English says vaguely that Taichi himself is 'the same.'

highlights.text: The thought that Taichi is the same

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "......"
adjudicated.assessment: The source text has multiple authoritative occurrences and this unit lacks a unique binding.

adjudicated.en: Dammit, so cute...
adjudicated.assessment: The English is supportable by the bound Japanese source in this unit.

adjudicated.jp: 「部活も頑張れ。仲間が死んでも頑張れ。大丈夫、来週には笑っていられっから」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Give it all on club, too. True Companions may die, but still give it all. You'll be all right, because next week you'll be all laughs."
adjudicated.assessment: Nanaka urges him to persist with the club even if companions die and says he will be able to smile next week. The English turns the concessive event into a possibility, invents a capitalized class, and changes smiling into being an object of laughter.

adjudicated.jp: 「うわ、不謹慎なこと言うなっ」
adjudicated.en: Taichi: "Whoa, don't say imprudent stuff!"
comments: See CCA0030. Hum, if Kenneth Broadcast Channel would reveal that everyone's insane, this reveals... -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: 不謹慎 means insensitive or inappropriate toward a grave subject. 'Imprudent' means merely unwise or incautious.

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "We got two dead dammiiit!"
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese says that two people are dead. The English turns 'dead' into an unheaded count noun, uses a possession construction, and adds a curse.

adjudicated.jp: 「あー、一応言っとくとあたしが殺したんじゃないよ？」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Ahhh, just in case, I'ma telling you that I didn't kill them, right?"
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese casually clarifies that she was not the killer. The English combines incompatible progressive and infinitival slang forms and adds a performative 'telling you.'

adjudicated.jp: 「えーーーーーーーーーーーっ！？」
adjudicated.en: Taichi: "EHHHHHHHHHHHH?!"
adjudicated.assessment: The English is supportable by the bound Japanese source in this unit.

adjudicated.jp: 「……あたしが殺したと確信していたね、キミ？」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "...you were sure I had killed them, weren't ya?"
adjudicated.assessment: The English is supportable by the bound Japanese source in this unit.

adjudicated.jp: 「なんかさ、不思議な力持ってそうだし、アリバイとかトリックとか超越して自由に殺せるんじゃないの？　神殺人事件とか言ってさ。推理小説でも何でもないけど」
adjudicated.en: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."
comments: Eight people, no one else - no one else at all... isn't this just the ultimate closed room mystery in a sense? But if the culprit is chance... then at the very least, it having been picked to be 'chance' is not, itself, random. This is Blessed Luck, meaning the culprit is, in that lateral and not-straightforwards sense, indeed God. This also hints at the motive: since no one dies, death alone can't be the point at all. This is subtly but pervasively anti-nihilistic. -GHS
adjudicated.assessment: The English dialogue is missing its opening quotation mark, duplicates 'you,' and renders 自由に殺せる as being 'free' or permitted to murder rather than able to kill without ordinary constraints.

highlights.text: Taichi: Well, yannow, when it looks like you have inexplicable powers, couldn't you you transcend alibis and tricks and all that and be free to murder? It could be said to be a Murder by God. Not that it's a whodunit novel or anything though."

adjudicated.jp: 「うーん、神ってのは近いかもね、けっこう」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Huuum, God might be close I guess, and very much so."
adjudicated.assessment: 神 is generic here and does not require capitalized 'God.' The appended coordination 'and very much so' is also ungrammatical for けっこう, which modifies how close the comparison is.

highlights.text: God might be close I guess, and very much so

adjudicated.jp: 「ひもパンいる？　あげようか？」

adjudicated.assessment: ひもパン means string panties, not jams.

adjudicated.jp: 「ううん、いらない。もらってもソッコー捨てる」
adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Nope, don'wann'em. Gimme that stuff and I'll just boom throw it away."
adjudicated.assessment: The Japanese says she does not want them and would throw them away immediately if given them. The English uses malformed contractions, changes a hypothetical receipt to an imperative, and invents 'boom.'

highlights.text: don'wann'em. Gimme that stuff and I'll just boom throw it away

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "Dooo you now..."
adjudicated.assessment: そーかい means 'Is that so' or 'I see.' The English asks an incomplete question about what she does.

adjudicated.en: Nanaka: "Going home now. Bye."
adjudicated.assessment: The English is supportable by the bound Japanese source in this unit.

adjudicated.jp: どこに帰っているんだろう、七香は。
adjudicated.en: where would Nanaka even go home to?
adjudicated.assessment: Taichi wonders where she habitually goes home. The conditional 'would go' instead frames a hypothetical destination.

adjudicated.en: Taichi: "Bai bai."
adjudicated.assessment: The source uses the familiar loan ばいばい as ordinary Japanese for 'bye-bye.' Re-romanizing it instead of giving the English expression creates an unnecessary untranslated surface.
